title: How Guest Reviews Shape Where Travelers Stay Now
seoTitle: How Guest Reviews Shape Where Travelers Stay
seoDescription: How hotel and resort reviews are read by travelers and summarized by Google and AI assistants, which themes matter most, and how to respond to reviews well.
excerpt: Travelers still read your reviews, but Google and AI tools now boil them down into a few themes first. Here is what that means for resorts and hotels.
imageAlt: Hotel guest in a white bathrobe sitting up in bed, reading on her smartphone
imageIdea: Real photo of a guest in a hotel room checking a phone, natural light, screen not readable, no brand logos.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
Guest reviews now shape where travelers stay in two ways. Travelers still read them directly to decide whether a hotel or resort is worth the price, and Google and AI assistants increasingly boil them down into a few themes, such as the pool, the spa, check in or surprise fees, that a traveler sees before reading a single review. The themes that repeat across your reviews become your short description, whether you like it or not.

That makes reviews an operations issue as much as a marketing one. What guests keep mentioning is what travelers will be told about you.

What do travelers actually look for in hotel reviews?

They look for patterns and for the details that matter to their trip. A family wants to know if the pool is crowded and the rooms are quiet. A couple wants to know if the spa is worth it and the view matches the photos. A business traveler wants fast check in and reliable Wi-Fi. One complaint is noise. The same complaint ten times is a fact.

They also read your replies. A 2019 Tripadvisor study conducted by Ipsos MORI, which surveyed more than 23,000 Tripadvisor users in 12 markets, found that 77% said they were more likely to book when an owner leaves personalized responses to reviews, and 89% said a thoughtful response to a negative review improved their impression of the business. The research is a few years old, but nothing about how guests read replies has made them matter less.

How do Google and AI tools summarize your reviews?

They group what guests write into recurring themes and present those themes up front. Google's help page on business summaries on Google Maps describes place topics, which are main themes based on the reviews of a business and only appear once a business has enough reviews. The same page notes that some hotels show review summaries licensed from TrustYou, a third party that aggregates reviews from across the web.

Google has also added AI written summaries. When Google brought Gemini features to Maps in late 2024, coverage of the launch described a review summary shown under a place's ratings and a box that lets people ask questions about the place. More recently, Skift reported that Google's AI Mode lets travelers describe a trip and compare hotels with prices, photos, amenities and reviews side by side. Assistants such as ChatGPT and Perplexity do something similar when they describe a hotel using what they find on review sites and the open web.

The practical result looks like this:

What guests keep writingWhat a summary may say
"The pool was packed by 10am"Pool can get crowded
"Best massage I have had, the spa team was lovely"Guests praise the spa
"Waited 40 minutes to check in"Some guests report slow check in
"Resort fee was not clear when I booked"Some guests mention unexpected fees
"Staff remembered our names all week"Staff described as friendly and attentive

No owner can edit those lines. They change only when the underlying reviews change, which means they change when the experience does.

Which review themes matter most for resorts and hotels?

The ones tied to why guests chose you and the ones tied to friction. For a resort, the first group is usually the pool, the beach, the spa, the food and the view. The second group is check in, cleanliness, noise, parking and fees.

Fees deserve their own mention. A resort fee that a guest did not expect turns a good stay into a review about feeling misled, and that theme spreads into summaries quickly. The fix is not in the reply. It is being clear about the total price before the guest books.

I encourage owners to read their reviews by theme rather than by star rating. A 4.6 average can hide a slow check in pattern that is already shaping how AI tools describe you. A few 3 star reviews that all praise the spa can tell you what to feature in your photos and your marketing.

How should a hotel respond to reviews?

Respond like the next guest is reading, because they are. Good replies are specific, human and short. They show that a real person read the review and that the property listens.

  • Use the details. Mention the spa treatment, the anniversary or the room they stayed in. Copy and paste replies read as indifference.
  • Own the problem without arguing. If check in was slow, say so and say what has changed. Do not debate the timeline in public.
  • Keep private matters private. Never share booking details, room numbers or anything a guest told your staff in confidence.
  • Offer a direct line. For serious complaints, invite the guest to contact a named manager.
  • Thank good reviews properly. A specific thank you to a happy guest tells future guests what you are proud of.

A reply will not change what a summary says about a recurring problem. Fixing the problem will, and your replies are where you show travelers you have done it.

How do you get more reviews without breaking the rules?

Ask every guest, at the right moment, with nothing attached. Google's prohibited and restricted content policy does not allow incentivized reviews, and Google also prohibits offering incentives to change or remove a negative review. A free drink, a discount or an upgrade in exchange for a review puts your profile at risk.

Volume and freshness matter because Google says review count and score factor into local ranking, in its guide on how to improve local ranking. A steady flow of honest reviews also keeps summaries current, so a problem you fixed last spring does not keep defining you this winter.

What does good look like?

Good looks like a steady flow of recent reviews on Google and the travel sites your guests use, replies to most of them within a few days, and themes that match what you want to be known for. When you read the summary of your hotel on Google or ask an AI assistant about you, it should sound like the stay you are proud of, not the one you had two years ago.

This is part of the work we do for resorts, hotels and boutique stays at The SocialDM, alongside Google Search, Google Maps and AI answers. You can see how it fits together on our hospitality marketing page. Your team owns the guest experience. We make sure what travelers read about it is current, consistent and working in your favor.

Questions we hear

Do hotel reviews still matter if Google and AI tools summarize them?

More than ever. A summary is built from what guests actually wrote, so the themes that repeat across your reviews become the short description travelers see first. You cannot edit the summary, but you can change what guests keep writing about.

Should a hotel reply to every review?

Reply to as many as you reasonably can, positive and negative, and make each reply specific. In a 2019 Tripadvisor study, 77% of travelers said personalized owner responses made them more likely to book.

How should a hotel respond to a bad review?

Thank the guest, acknowledge the specific issue, say what you have done or changed, and offer a direct way to follow up. Stay calm and avoid arguing about details in public. Future guests are the real audience.

Can we offer guests a discount or upgrade for leaving a review?

Not on Google. Google's policy prohibits incentivized reviews, and also prohibits offering incentives to change or remove a negative review. Ask every guest the same way, with nothing attached.

Do reviews affect where a hotel ranks on Google Maps?

Yes. Google says review count and review score factor into local ranking, alongside relevance and distance.
